channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The Bank of Japan kept its short-term rate at 1.25%, the highest since April 1995, in an 8–1 vote and said for the first time that its 2% inflation target has been reached, Il Sole 24 Ore reports.
item.description:
Il Sole 24 Ore reports that the Bank of Japan kept its short-term policy rate at 1.25%, as markets expected, with eight votes in favour and one against. The decision followed two consecutive increases of 25 basis points, in June and September, and borrowing costs are at their highest level since April 1995. The Bank also stated for the first time that its 2% inflation target has now been reached, more than 13 years after the target was set. The Economic Times says the Bank signalled the possibility of an increase later this year, and that the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve left the door open to a rate rise at their final meetings of the year in December. Cnyes reports that the Bank of Canada raised its rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% in the same week and that traders expect central banks in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Sweden and Norway to tighten further while energy prices stand at multi-month highs. The rows do not give the dissenting member's view, inflation figures or the Bank's projections.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a decision to hold and a statement on inflation, not a new rate path. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a policy rate at its highest level since 1995 together with a signal of a possible increase would keep borrowing costs elevated for Japanese industry and housing, and the same direction in other central banks points to a wider period of tight money. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Japanese customers in automotive and electronics buy bonding and sealing materials, so higher financing costs could slow investment decisions, while the rows give no figures for materials or orders. Points that may be worth considering include the Bank's next meeting, Japanese inflation data and the December meetings of the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve.

Il Sole 24 Ore | The Economic Times | Cnyes

item.title: The German Economic Institute IW says the US goods trade deficit reached USD 130 billion in August, above its level two years earlier despite tariffs, though the EU's share fell to 7% from 20% in August 2024 and China's to 14% from 29%.
item.description:
MarketScreener, The News International and The Standard report on a study by the German Economic Institute IW, which finds that President Trump's economic agenda has delivered solid growth and strong investment in some sectors but has not reduced the trade deficit. In August the US goods trade deficit was USD 130 billion, above its level two years earlier despite broad import tariffs. The EU's share of the deficit fell to 7% from 20% in August 2024; China's share fell to 14% from 29%, with no date given for the earlier figure. Foreign direct investment inflows fell 8.2% to USD 248 billion in 2025, about 18% below the average for 2015 to 2024. The News International adds that growth was supported in part by investment in artificial intelligence, that job creation lagged the previous administration and that inflation stayed above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. The Standard says the US–Israeli war against Iran is adding to already high public debt and pushing up interest rates, with creditors questioning whether the country can sustain debt of USD 40 trillion. The rows do not say which countries' shares rose, which tariff rates lie behind the figures, or what the study forecasts.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report one month of trade data and an annual investment figure, not tariff revenue or import volumes by product. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a deficit that stays high while the EU and Chinese shares fall suggests that imports have shifted to other origins rather than fallen, which would mean that tariffs change supply routes more than they reduce total import demand. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, customers and suppliers in chemicals and manufacturing buy and sell across borders, so rerouted trade and lower foreign investment could change sourcing and plant decisions, while the rows give no figures for chemicals or materials. Points that may be worth considering include the US trade data for September, new US tariff measures expected after the midterm elections and US inflows of foreign direct investment in 2026.

MarketScreener | The News International | The Standard

item.title: Xi Jinping and Swiss President Guy Parmelin signed the upgraded China–Switzerland free trade agreement in Beijing on 30 October, under which 99.8% of Swiss exports are eventually to enter China duty free, up from around 53.6%, Chinatimes reports.
item.description:
Chinatimes reports that Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Swiss President Guy Parmelin signed the upgraded free trade agreement in Beijing on 30 October. The revision addresses the imbalance of the original 2014 agreement and adds content such as digital trade, investment access, labour protection and environmental protection. Under it, 99.8% of Swiss exports to mainland China are eventually to enter duty free, up from around 53.6%, with 77.5% covered from the date the agreement takes effect, including watches, precision instruments, machinery, pharmaceuticals and chemicals. Les Echos says the 99.8% is to be reached over the next ten years, up from around 50%, that Swiss watches become duty free but still carry the Chinese consumption tax on luxury goods, that Swiss access widens in several sectors, including manufacturing services, aircraft maintenance and maritime transport, and that Swiss duties are to be removed on 97.3% of Chinese agricultural exports, up from 80.1%. Xhby.net says two new chapters cover digital trade and trade and sustainable development, and that China will relax sectoral restrictions on manufacturing-related services, professional design, finance, maritime and air transport. The rows give no date for entry into force, no ratification steps and no tariff rates for chemicals.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a signed agreement, not one in force, and they give no tariff lines for chemicals. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, an agreement that removes duties on chemicals and machinery lowers costs for Swiss exporters to China, and it changes the price position of their products against suppliers from other countries that still pay duty. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, suppliers of chemicals and machinery compete across borders in China, so duty-free access for Swiss products could shift relative prices in some product groups, while the rows give no figures for adhesives or related materials. Points that may be worth considering include the date of entry into force, the tariff schedule for chemicals and the machinery covered from the date the agreement takes effect.

Chinatimes.com | Les Echos | Xhby.net

item.title: Cotality reports that Australian home values fell 1.2% in October, the seventh consecutive monthly fall, to 2.8% below a year earlier and 6.7% below their peak, while sales fell 23% from a year earlier.
item.description:
ABC, MarketScreener and Xinhua report, citing the property data firm Cotality, that Australia's national home values fell 1.2% in October, the seventh consecutive monthly decline, and are down 2.8% on a year earlier. MarketScreener adds that values are 6.7% below their peak and that capital-city values were falling at their fastest in 40 years, with prices down 8.1% in seven months, while sales fell 23% from a year earlier and are 18% below the five-year average. Xinhua says the median capital-city house price fell 1.4%, faster than the 1.2% fall in September. Brisbane fell 2.0% in the month, Perth 1.7% and Sydney 1.6%, while Hobart and Darwin recorded moderate gains. Cotality's research director Tim Lawless attributes the downturn to a range of headwinds including the federal government's move to wind back tax concessions for property investors, cost-of-living pressures, persistently low confidence and interest rate hikes. Finance News Network reports that the Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise its cash rate for the fifth time on 3 November, to 4.85%, an 18-year high. The rows give no figures for building approvals or construction activity.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report home values and sales, not construction starts or renovation spending. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, falling prices together with sales well below the five-year average and a further rate rise expected describe a housing market in which buyers are holding back, which can lower new-build demand with a lag. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, residential construction and renovation use bonding, sealing and coating materials, so a prolonged price fall could weigh on orders in Australia, while the rows give no figures for building activity or materials. Points that may be worth considering include the Reserve Bank's decision on 3 November, Australian building approvals and whether the monthly falls continue.

ABC | MarketScreener | Xinhua News | Finance News Network

item.title: Seven OPEC+ producers kept their December oil production targets unchanged at an online meeting on 1 November, signalling that it is unlikely to make further changes before next year, while most members still produce below target, LiveMint reports.
item.description:
LiveMint and China Economic Net report that seven OPEC+ members, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman, met online on 1 November and decided to keep production in December at the September level. The statement gave no reason; LiveMint says the group is unlikely to change its output policy until next year as the Iran war continues to disrupt oil exports from the Middle East, and that most members are producing well below their agreed targets, which limits the additional oil reaching the market. According to China Economic Net, the producers are to complete production capacity assessments in the fourth quarter to set quotas for 2027, and LiveMint notes that the United Arab Emirates, formerly part of the group's monthly decisions, left OPEC in May. The Hindu BusinessLine reports that Brent ended October at its highest level in six months and that oil prices fell more than 1% on 2 November as Iranian and Qatari officials held a third day of talks on ending the war. The rows give no production volumes, no target figures and no estimate of spare capacity.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report an unchanged decision and a price move on one day, not production data. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, an unchanged target at a time when most members produce below target adds little supply, so the oil price depends more on the disruption to Middle East exports and on the talks to end the war than on the group's policy. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, oil is the starting point for petrochemical raw materials, so a price that stays near a six-month high could keep resin and solvent costs elevated, while the rows give no figures for these. Points that may be worth considering include the group's quota decisions for 2027, Brent after the Iran–Qatar talks and price reports for ethylene, propylene and resins.

LiveMint | China Economic Net | The Hindu Business Line

item.title: French new passenger car registrations rose 7% to 149,340 in October despite one fewer working day than a year earlier, while vehicle registrations in the first ten months were 4.4% higher, Les Echos reports.
item.description:
Les Echos reports that new passenger car registrations in France reached 149,340 in October 2026, 7% more than a year earlier, according to the Plateforme Automobile (PFA), even though the month had one working day fewer than October 2025. In the first ten months about 1,384,293 vehicles were registered, 4.4% more than in the same period last year. The article says hybrid vehicles hold the largest market share at 44% and electric vehicles account for 41% of sales; it does not state whether these shares refer to October or to the year to date. The best-selling electric models of the month were the Renault Twingo IV with 4,747 registrations, the Renault 5 with 4,666 and the Peugeot 208 with 3,221. The row gives no figures for the share of Chinese brands, for production, for orders or for the effect of prices on registrations.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports registrations, not production or orders. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, registrations that grow despite one fewer working day indicate firm demand in October, and a large share of hybrid and electric models changes the mix of parts that carmakers buy. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, automotive manufacturing uses bonding, sealing and coating materials, and electric-vehicle platforms add battery and lightweight-body bonding, so a rising electric share could change demand by product, while the row gives no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include French registrations for November, registration data for other European markets and the market share of Chinese brands.

Les Echos

item.title: German GDP rose 0.2% in the third quarter from the second on preliminary data, above the 0.1% economists expected, the Federal Statistical Office said, while the euro area grew 0.4% and France contracted 0.1%.
item.description:
According to the Federal Statistical Office, as reported by Handelsblatt, Wallstreet:online and the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, German GDP rose 0.2% in the third quarter from the second on preliminary data, against an expected 0.1%. Handelsblatt says low water levels on the Rhine slowed inland shipping and disrupted industrial supply chains, foreign trade was weaker, and consumers gave little impetus because of high energy prices. The FAZ says the recovery slowed from a good first half but did not stall, that consumption rose slightly, which it says may be due mainly to government spending, and that economists expect stronger growth in the fourth quarter. Wallstreet:online says the economy is expected to keep growing at a moderate pace in the coming quarters, that the lack of radical reforms is likely to keep corporate investment from recovering significantly, and that exports are not expected to recover as strongly as usual because of US tariffs and Chinese competition. Daily Sabah, citing a Reuters poll, reports euro-area growth of 0.4% against 0.6% in the second quarter and an expected 0.2%, with Spain and the Netherlands at 0.6%, Italy unchanged and France at minus 0.1%. La Tribune says French exports fell 1.7% after a 2.8% rise, with transport equipment, particularly aeronautics, down 9.1% after a 20.8% rise. The rows do not give the German breakdown by sector, revisions of earlier quarters or an official forecast.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report one quarter of preliminary data, not a forecast for the year. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, growth of 0.2% after low Rhine water and high energy prices describes an economy that is expanding slowly, and a euro area that grows faster than Germany and France suggests that demand is uneven across countries. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, German and French manufacturing and construction customers use bonding, sealing and coating materials, so slow growth in Germany and weaker French investment and exports could weigh on orders, while the rows give no figures for materials or for construction output. Points that may be worth considering include the Federal Statistical Office's breakdown of investment and construction, German industrial orders and the business surveys for November.

Handelsblatt | Wallstreet:online | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Daily Sabah | La Tribune

item.title: The Ifo Institute expects 195,000 completed apartments in Germany in each of 2027 and 2028, below its February forecasts of 205,000 and 215,000, which an Ifo expert attributes to costs that kept rising because of the Iran war, the FAZ reports.
item.description:
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports that the Ifo Institute expects housing construction in Germany to make little progress despite faster approvals, with fewer than 200,000 apartments completed in each of the next two years, specifically 195,000 in 2027 and 195,000 in 2028. In February the institute had expected 205,000 completions in 2027 and 215,000 in 2028. Ifo construction expert Ludwig Dorffmeister told the Augsburger Allgemeine that the forecasts had to be revised down because construction costs continued to rise as a result of the Iran war. Completions this year are expected to fall, as forecast, to a 15-year low of 185,000, which is 20,000 fewer than in 2025. The FAZ cites an analysis by the Federal Institute for Research on Building, Urban Affairs and Spatial Development that around 320,000 new apartments are needed each year by 2030. The row gives no figures for approvals, building permits or construction costs, no breakdown by type of building, and no reason why faster approvals have not yet lifted completions.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a forecast by one institute and a needs estimate by a federal institute, not completed-building data for 2027 or 2028. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, forecast completions of 195,000 in 2027 and 2028 against a need of around 320,000 a year by 2030 describe a gap that could persist for several years, and costs that rise faster than expected can delay projects that are already approved. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, new apartment construction uses bonding, sealing and coating materials, so completions that stay low could limit volumes in German new-build, while renovation work may follow a different pattern, and the row gives no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include German building permits and construction orders, the Ifo residential construction climate and the next revision of the Ifo forecast.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: China's official manufacturing PMI fell 0.8 points to 49.3 in October, and the construction activity index in the non-manufacturing PMI fell 2.3 points to 48.0, the National Bureau of Statistics reported; a private survey showed 52.0.
item.description:
The National Bureau of Statistics reports that China's official manufacturing purchasing managers' index fell 0.8 points to 49.3 in October from 50.1, which Chinatimes describes as a three-month low and CNA as the third contraction in four months. The production index was 49.8, down 1.9 points, and the new orders index 49.4, down 1.1 points. The index for large enterprises was 50.2, down 0.4 points, while those for medium-sized and small enterprises were 48.4 and 47.5, down 1.3 and 1.4 points. High-tech manufacturing stood at 51.3 and equipment manufacturing at 50.6, both above the 50-point line that separates expansion from contraction. Huo Lihui, chief statistician of the Bureau's Service Industry Survey Center, attributed the fall to some demand being released before the National Day holiday and to the complex and volatile international environment. The non-manufacturing index fell 0.5 points to 49.7 from 50.2; Xinhua reports that the services index fell 0.2 points to 50.0 and the construction business activity index fell 2.3 points to 48.0, and the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing, in an analysis based on the Bureau's survey, puts the non-manufacturing new orders index at 44.4, down 2.1 points. A private manufacturing PMI from S&P Global and RatingDog fell 0.1 points to 52.0, its eleventh month above 50. The rows do not give the previous construction index or an explanation of why the two manufacturing surveys differ.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report survey indices for one month, not output, orders in value terms or construction starts. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a construction activity index at 48.0 after a fall of 2.3 points, together with a non-manufacturing new orders index at 44.4 that also covers services, point to weaker activity at the end of the quarter, and demand brought forward before the holiday is a timing effect that one month cannot separate from a trend. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction and manufacturing customers in China use bonding, sealing and coating materials, so lower activity indices could point to softer orders, while the two manufacturing surveys point in different directions and the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the November readings of both manufacturing surveys, the construction index in the coming months, and Chinese housing and investment data.

CNA | Chinatimes.com | Xinhua News | People's Daily Online | CFLP | Commercial Times

item.title: AF&PA says the US containerboard operating rate stayed above 94.5% for a second consecutive quarter, 2.5 points above last year to date, and mill inventories ended it below 370,000 short tons, a first since October 2024.
item.description:
The American Forest & Paper Association (AF&PA) reports that the total US containerboard operating rate stayed above 94.5% for the second consecutive quarter, which puts the year-to-date rate 2.5 points above last year. Containerboard production in the third quarter rose 2.7% from the second quarter, while new supply, defined as production minus exports plus imports, rose 5.8%. Exports fell 11% from the second quarter and imports rose 25%. The recycled medium operating rate rose to 95.1% compared with the second quarter and is more than 4 points above its prior year-to-date level, while the operating rates for linerboard grades and semichemical medium declined slightly from the second quarter but stayed in the mid-90s. Mill inventories ended the quarter below 370,000 short tons, the first time since October 2024. The release gives no figures for capacity, for demand by end use or for prices, and it gives no reason for the rise in imports.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The release reports mill operating rates, supply and inventories, not box demand or prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, operating rates in the mid-90s together with inventories below 370,000 short tons describe tight supply at the mills, and imports that rise while exports fall point to more of the supply coming from abroad in the quarter. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, corrugated packaging is converted and closed with adhesives, so the volume that passes through containerboard mills can indicate demand for packaging adhesives, while the release gives no figures for the converting stage. Points that may be worth considering include box shipment data, containerboard prices and the association's next quarterly report.

American Forest & Paper Association

item.title: Freight for oil shipped from Russia's western ports to India stayed at record highs in late October, with an Aframax cargo from Baltic ports at about USD 23 million per one-way voyage against USD 13–16 million in September, MarketScreener reports.
item.description:
MarketScreener, citing three trading and shipping sources, reports that freight rates for oil shipped from Russia's western ports to India remained at record highs in late October, reflecting risks in the Black Sea and a shortage of vessels amid disruptions and strong global demand. An Aframax tanker carrying about 100,000 metric tons from Russia's Baltic ports to western India costs around USD 23 million per one-way voyage, against roughly USD 13 million to USD 16 million in September, and a Suezmax tanker can be fixed for the same route at about USD 27 million. Shipping Urals crude from the Black Sea to India on a Suezmax tanker of about 140,000 tons costs a record USD 30 million per one-way voyage, up from around USD 19 million in September. Bloomberg describes, in a separate piece, how Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on each other's export industries over the past year, with Kyiv striking refineries, oil terminals and tankers as well as Russian grain hubs on the Black Sea and ships, and Russia targeting ports, elevators, warehouses, ships and other infrastructure critical to Ukrainian agriculture. The rows do not give freight rates for other routes, the value of the cargoes, how much of the cost reaches the price of refined products, or an outlook for rates.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report freight quotes for two tanker classes on two routes, not the price of oil or of the products made from it. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, freight that has moved from USD 13–16 million to USD 23 million per Aframax voyage adds to the delivered cost of crude, and a shortage of vessels can keep rates high whatever the oil price does. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, many raw materials are derived from petrochemicals, so higher delivered crude costs could feed into resin and solvent prices with a lag, while the rows give no figures for these. Points that may be worth considering include freight quotes for other routes and ship sizes, spot prices for monomers and resins, and any change in attacks on tankers and ports in the Black Sea.

MarketScreener | Bloomberg
